structure.title: Table of Contents
structure.summary:
The document outlines the architecture and design of an SDK-based plugin platform for agents. It begins with an overview of the SDK architecture, including the execution model and Plugin Gateway pipeline, followed by a detailed security model describing five layers of isolation and enforcement points.

It defines the Agent Interface Contract, covering the manifest specification and core methods such as `execute()` and `onFeedback()`, and explains the Platform Access APIs for controlled state read/write, knowledge base access, history, and LLM integration. The UI Rendering Contract specifies supported UI components (Card, Table, Form, File, Custom Component), while the Plugin Output Bus enables inter-plugin communication.

The document also describes the representative interface layout, including plugin rendering areas and the Customer Context Panel, and details eight built-in quick action plugins with their triggers, data flows, outputs, and LLM usage. Governance topics include agent manifest control (versioning, customization, domain-agnostic design), feedback and analytics mechanisms, and the full plugin lifecycle from development to monitoring.

It concludes with an alternative open plugin framework approach and a summary of key technical decisions guiding the platform’s design.

structure.title: Module 12: Quick Action Agent SDK — Plugin Framework
structure.prefix_summary: Module 12 defines the Quick Action Agent SDK, establishing the standardized plugin framework used by both built-in and custom plugins. It outlines the Agent Interface Contract (manifest, execution, feedback), scoped Platform Access APIs, UI rendering templates (Card, Table, Form), inter-plugin communication via the Plugin Output Bus, and the complete plugin lifecycle from development to monitoring. The document clarifies that built-in plugins and custom plugins use the exact same SDK, ensuring consistency and robustness. It distinguishes between MVP capabilities—8 built-in plugins, limited UI templates, read-only state access, no third-party development—and the full product vision, which adds custom plugin development, sandboxed state write access, custom UI components, plugin review workflows, marketplace distribution, and external LLM connectors. It also explains the two developer audiences: internal engineers and tenant developers, both governed by the same security and gateway enforcement model, with custom plugins requiring review before activation.

nodes.title: 12.1 SDK Architecture Overview
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.1 SDK Architecture Overview

The Plugin Agent SDK is NOT a standalone library that runs anywhere. It is an interface contract plus a runtime sandbox that lives inside the platform. Think of it like a Shopify App SDK or Slack Bolt framework — you build to a defined interface, and the platform executes your code within its controlled environment. The plugin never runs independently; the Orchestrator (Module 2) invokes it through the Plugin Gateway.

nodes.title: 12.1.1 Execution Model
nodes.summary:
The document section describes the execution model for plugins within the Orchestrator system, detailing the full lifecycle of plugin execution from trigger to logging.

It begins with trigger evaluation, where the Orchestrator checks whether a plugin’s automatic trigger conditions are met or whether a user manually activates it. Once selected for execution, the Plugin Gateway assembles a strictly scoped execution context based on the plugin’s manifest. This includes required session state fields, knowledge base data (if specified), conversation history up to a defined depth, prior plugin outputs, and an LLM client when required.

Plugins execute in a sandboxed, isolated environment with no direct access to databases, core modules, or cross-tenant data. Execution is time-limited, with configurable maximum duration per plugin.

After execution, the system validates the plugin’s output against its declared schema. Invalid outputs (e.g., wrong structure or unsafe content) are rejected and replaced with a fallback error card. Valid outputs are then sanitized to remove unsafe elements such as scripts or external resource links before being stored for inter-plugin access and sent to the UI.

The system logs detailed analytics for each execution, including execution time, token usage, state reads, knowledge base queries, output type, and trigger type. These metrics feed into a feedback and optimization module.

The section also includes a reference implementation of the execution pipeline in code and explains plugin initialization behavior at session start. At the beginning of a session, all enabled tenant plugins are loaded, and those configured with automatic surface triggers may execute immediately. Plugins operate independently, and their load order does not affect functionality.

nodes.title: 12.2 Security Model — Five Layers of Isolation
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the **Security Model for the Plugin System**, defining a **Five-Layer Isolation Framework** designed to ensure that plugins cannot compromise tenant data, system integrity, or platform security. The core philosophy is defense-in-depth: if one layer fails, the remaining layers still prevent a breach.

### Core Security Objectives
A plugin must never be able to:
- Access another tenant’s data
- Corrupt core conversation or agent state
- Inject malicious UI content
- Make undeclared external network calls
- Escalate its own permissions

---

## Five Layers of Isolation

### 1. Sandboxed Execution
Plugins run in isolated environments (separate function invocation or container/Lambda). They cannot import core modules, access raw databases, or interact directly with internal systems.  
**Prevents:** Direct state access, SQL reads, file system access, Orchestrator internals access.  
**Enforced by:** Plugin Gateway provisioning a clean execution environment per invocation.

---

### 2. Scoped API Access
Plugins interact strictly through a controlled `PluginContext` object. All state reads, knowledge base queries, and history access pass through the Plugin Gateway, which enforces:
- Tenant isolation
- Field-level permissions
- Rate limits

**Prevents:** Cross-tenant data access, access to auth tokens or agent internals, and resource abuse.  
**Enforced by:** Plugin Gateway validation of all API calls.

---

### 3. State Write Sandboxing
Plugins can only write to their own namespace:
```
plugin_state.{own_plugin_id}.*
```
Writes to core state areas (agent_state, discovery, customer, recommendations) are rejected.  
**Prevents:** Corruption of conversation state, customer data, or system logic.  
**Enforced by:** State Engine validation of every write request.

---

### 4. Output Sanitization
Plugin output is sanitized before being rendered in the UI. Only structured JSON templates (Card/Table/Form) are allowed. No raw HTML, scripts, event handlers, or external resource URLs are permitted.  
**Prevents:** XSS attacks, DOM manipulation, content injection, tracking pixels, malware.  
**Enforced by:** Plugin Gateway sanitization and strict UI rendering rules.

---

### 5. Review Gate (Full Product Only)
Custom plugins must pass review before activation, including:
- Manifest audit
- Code review
- Security scanning
- Test harness validation

Only plugins marked as `approved` can move to `active`.  
**Prevents:** Malicious plugins, data exfiltration, undeclared network calls, excessive permissions.  
**Enforced by:** Plugin registry lifecycle controls.

---

## Resource Limits & Rate Limiting
The Plugin Gateway enforces per-execution limits:
- 10 state reads
- 3 knowledge base queries
- 1 LLM call
- 5-second timeout

Exceeding limits terminates execution and returns a fallback error card. Limits are configurable via the plugin manifest (`resourceLimits` field).

---

## Architectural Decision

The **Plugin Gateway resides within Module 2 (Orchestrator)** rather than being a separate service. It extends the agent execution pipeline with plugin-specific sandboxing and permission checks.

**Rationale:**
- Plugin execution mirrors agent execution (context in → structured output out).
- Reuses existing infrastructure for context assembly and state management.
- Avoids unnecessary service complexity.
- Can be extracted into a standalone service if plugin volume increases in the future.

---

Overall, the document defines a robust, layered security architecture that combines execution isolation, strict API mediation, namespace-restricted state writes, UI sanitization, and governance review to ensure plugins cannot compromise platform integrity.

nodes.title: 12.3.1 The Manifest
nodes.summary:
The document explains that every plugin—whether built-in or custom—is defined by a JSON manifest that specifies all operational, behavioral, and resource details required by the platform.

It outlines that the manifest includes:

- **Basic metadata** such as ID, name, version, icon, and description.
- **Trigger configuration**, including automatic trigger conditions based on system state, manual triggering options, auto-surfacing behavior, and UI priority.
- **State and knowledge base requirements**, specifying which internal state fields and external knowledge sources the plugin needs, along with retrieval limits.
- **Conversation context depth**, defining how much prior conversation history is available to the plugin.
- **LLM configuration**, including whether an LLM is required, model selection, token limits, and temperature settings.
- **Output schema**, describing the structure of the plugin’s output (e.g., a form with defined fields).
- **Permissions model**, detailing what state data can be read or written, knowledge base access rights, and whether external network access is allowed.
- **Resource limits**, such as execution time, state reads, knowledge base queries, and LLM call limits.
- **Feedback collection**, specifying which user interaction signals are tracked and whether feedback triggers additional behavior.

Overall, the section defines the manifest as a comprehensive contract that governs a plugin’s functionality, data access, UI behavior, execution constraints, and feedback mechanisms.

nodes.title: 12.3.2 Manifest Field Reference
nodes.summary:
This section defines the **Plugin Manifest Field Reference**, outlining all required and optional configuration fields that govern how a plugin behaves, what it can access, and how it is controlled within the platform.

The main points covered include:

- **Plugin Identification & Triggering**
  - Each plugin has a unique `id` with strict naming conventions.
  - Plugins can activate automatically via `triggerConditions` or manually via `manualTrigger`.
  - `surfacePriority` determines display order when multiple plugins activate simultaneously.

- **Data & Context Access Control**
  - `stateRequirements` strictly define which state fields a plugin can access.
  - `conversationHistoryDepth` limits how much prior conversation context is available.
  - `kbRequirements` configure knowledge base access if needed.
  - The Plugin Gateway enforces declared access and blocks undeclared usage.

- **LLM & Output Configuration**
  - `llmRequired` and `llmConfig` specify whether a language model is used and how (model, tokens, temperature).
  - `outputSchema` defines the structure and type of the plugin’s output (e.g., card, table, form), which is validated by the Gateway.

- **Permissions & Security**
  - The `permissions` field explicitly declares allowed read/write access to state, KB access, and external network usage.
  - All permissions are enforced by the Gateway and reviewed during approval.

- **Execution Constraints**
  - `resourceLimits` define operational caps (timeout, state reads, KB queries, LLM calls).
  - The Gateway enforces hard limits to prevent abuse or overconsumption.

- **Feedback & Learning**
  - The `feedback` configuration specifies which user engagement signals to collect.
  - These signals feed into a broader feedback system for performance improvement.

Overall, this section establishes a structured, secure, and governable framework for defining plugin behavior, access rights, resource usage, and integration with LLMs and feedback systems.

nodes.title: 12.3.3 The execute() Function
nodes.summary:
This section explains the **`execute()` function**, which serves as the core logic of a plugin. It describes how the function:

- **Receives a `PluginContext` object**, which provides access to all provisioned data, including:
  - Declared state fields
  - Knowledge base (KB) results
  - Conversation history
  - LLM client
  - Outputs from other plugins

- **Accesses structured state data**, such as customer profile information, agent recommendations, and contact details.

- **Reads outputs from other plugins** using `context.pluginOutputs.read()` to incorporate related data (e.g., competitor comparisons).

- **Queries the knowledge base** via `context.kb.search()` to retrieve relevant supporting materials (e.g., case studies).

- **Calls an LLM through a built-in connector** using `context.llm.call()` to generate dynamic content (in this case, an email draft).

- **Returns a structured output** that conforms to the declared `outputSchema`. The example demonstrates returning a form UI configuration containing:
  - Pre-filled fields (recipient, subject, tone, body)
  - Configurable options (dropdown tone selection)
  - Action buttons (e.g., copy draft, regenerate)

Overall, the section illustrates how `execute()` orchestrates data retrieval, cross-plugin integration, knowledge lookup, LLM generation, and structured UI output creation within a plugin.

nodes.title: 12.3.4 The onFeedback() Handler
nodes.summary:
The section explains the **`onFeedback()` handler**, an optional plugin hook designed for **real-time, session-scoped adaptation**. It activates when a sales representative interacts with a plugin’s output—such as dismissing, editing, or regenerating content—and allows the plugin to adjust its behavior during the current session only.

Key points covered:

- **Purpose and Scope**:  
  `onFeedback()` is not a long-term learning system. Its role is limited to immediate, in-session adjustments. Persistent, cross-session learning is handled separately by Module 16 (Feedback Engine).

- **Behavior Examples**:  
  - If a rep clicks **“Regenerate”**, the handler can increment a regeneration counter and store contextual data (such as tone) in session memory so the next execution attempts a different approach.  
  - If a rep **heavily edits** the output (e.g., high edit distance), the handler can flag that the template may need improvement within the session.

- **Session Memory Usage**:  
  The handler stores temporary adaptation signals (e.g., regeneration count, tone preference, heavy edit flag) in `context.sessionMemory`, which influences subsequent `execute()` calls during the same conversation.

- **Comparison with Module 16 (Feedback Engine)**:  
  - `onFeedback()` is **ephemeral and session-specific**, focused on micro-adaptation.  
  - **Module 16** is **persistent and aggregative**, analyzing signals across sessions, users, and tenants to detect patterns and recommend systemic improvements (e.g., prompt changes, trigger adjustments, plugin disabling).  
  - Both systems use the same feedback signals: `onFeedback()` processes them synchronously for immediate adaptation, while Module 16 logs them asynchronously for long-term optimization.

Overall, the section emphasizes the distinction between short-term adaptive behavior and long-term strategic learning within the system’s feedback architecture.

nodes.title: 12.4.1 State Read API — What Plugins Can and Cannot Read
nodes.summary:
This section defines the **State Read API access rules**, clearly outlining what plugins are allowed and not allowed to read within the system, along with the security rationale behind each decision.

### Main Points Covered

1. **Readable Data (Allowed Access)**
   Plugins can access structured, pre-approved customer and session data necessary to perform their functions, including:
   - **Customer profile information** (company name, industry, revenue, etc.)
   - **Owned products** for cross-sell analysis and quote generation
   - **Customer contacts** for email drafting and stakeholder mapping
   - **Precomputed enrichment metrics** (health scores, growth, benchmarks)
   - **Active agent state** such as recommendations, conversation phase, and talking points
   - **Discovery progress and dimension tracking**
   - **Intent signals** extracted from conversations (e.g., objections, competitor mentions)
   - **Their own plugin state**
   - **Rendered outputs from other plugins (read-only)** via a shared output bus

   The guiding principle is that plugins can read structured, safe, business-relevant data needed to generate outputs and collaborate with other plugins.

2. **Restricted Data (Denied Access)**
   Plugins are explicitly blocked from accessing sensitive or internal system data, including:
   - Authentication credentials (tokens, JWTs)
   - Tenant configuration and business rules
   - Other plugins’ private internal state
   - System prompts and orchestration logic
   - Raw database access, SQL queries, or direct connections

   These restrictions establish strict security and IP protection boundaries.

3. **Architectural Principles**
   - Plugins operate strictly on **data, not platform configuration**.
   - Business rules are enforced by the **Orchestrator**, not exposed to plugins.
   - Inter-plugin collaboration happens only through **rendered outputs**, not internal state sharing.
   - All data access is mediated through a secure API layer — no direct database access.

Overall, the section establishes a **clear security boundary model** that balances plugin capability with strict protection of authentication data, proprietary logic, and infrastructure internals.

nodes.title: 12.4.2 State Write API
nodes.summary:
### Description of Section 12.4.2 – State Write API

This section defines the write permissions model for plugins, clearly distinguishing between MVP and full product capabilities and enforcing strict state isolation.

**Key Points:**

- **MVP Restriction:** Plugins are completely read-only and cannot write to any system state.
- **Full Product Capability:** Plugins may write data only within their own sandboxed namespace:
  - `plugin_state.{own_plugin_id}.*`

This ensures plugins can persist their own data (e.g., saved drafts, comparison data for audits) without affecting core system logic.

### Strictly Prohibited Write Targets

Plugins are explicitly forbidden from writing to any core system state, including:

- **`agent_state.*`** – Protects core reasoning, workflow phases, and recommendations.
- **`discovery.*`** – Prevents interference with discovery tracking and automated phase transitions.
- **`customer.*`** – Maintains CRM-imported customer data as a trusted source of truth.
- **`active_workflow`** – Ensures only the Orchestrator can control agent switching.
- **`recommendations.*`** – Restricts recommendation generation to core agents only.
- **`intent_signals.*`** – Preserves integrity of NLU-generated intent signals.

### Overall Principle

The design enforces strict sandboxing and system integrity. Plugins can persist their own internal data but are structurally prevented from altering core reasoning, workflow control, customer data, recommendations, or intent processing.

nodes.title: 12.4.3 KB Query API and History Read API
nodes.summary:
### 12.4.3 KB Query API and History Read API

KB Query API: The plugin provides a search query string and optional filters (source type, max results). The Plugin Gateway routes the query to the tenant’s Foundry IQ Knowledge Base (Module 3) with the tenant’s retrieval effort setting. Results come back as title + content snippet + relevance score. The plugin CANNOT modify, add, or delete KB entries. Read-only.

History Read API: The plugin receives the last N messages of the current conversation (N = conversationHistoryDepth from manifest, max 50). Messages include role (user/assistant), content, and timestamp. System prompts are stripped. The plugin CANNOT read conversations from other sessions, other reps, or other tenants.

nodes.title: 12.4.4 LLM Connector
nodes.summary:
The section describes the **LLM Connector** architecture for plugins, detailing how plugins access large language models (LLMs) in both the MVP and full product versions.

Plugins that require natural language generation must declare `llmRequired: true` in their manifest. They access the platform’s LLM through `context.llm.call()`, which routes requests via a centralized LLM connector.

### Key Areas Covered:

**1. LLM Source**
- **MVP:** Only a built-in connector is allowed. The LLM model is determined by the tenant’s configuration, and plugins cannot choose or override the provider.
- **Full Product:** Plugins may either use the built-in connector or declare an external LLM connector in their manifest. External providers must be explicitly declared and whitelisted by the Gateway to ensure security and governance.

**2. Token Tracking and Cost Control**
- **MVP:** Token usage is tracked per plugin execution, logged in analytics, and charged to the tenant.
- **Full Product:** Adds per-plugin token budgets, allowing tenant administrators to enforce monthly usage limits.

**3. Prompt Injection Protection**
- **MVP:** Plugin prompts are wrapped in a system-controlled envelope to prevent overriding platform-level instructions.
- **Full Product:** Includes additional automated scanning for prompt injection patterns during plugin review.

**4. Streaming Support**
- **MVP:** No streaming; plugins receive the full LLM response at once, and the UI shows a loading indicator.
- **Full Product:** Optional streaming support for long-form responses, enabling progressive UI rendering as tokens arrive.

### Final Decision Summary
For the MVP, only the built-in LLM connector is allowed to ensure cost control, consistency, and security. In the full product, external connectors are permitted with manifest declaration and Gateway whitelisting, enabling specialized use cases while maintaining governance and visibility.

nodes.title: 12.5 UI Rendering Contract
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.5 UI Rendering Contract

| Design Principle Plugins output STRUCTURED DATA. The platform renders it. This separation ensures consistent UX across all plugins, prevents UI injection attacks, enables the platform to adapt rendering for different devices (desktop sidebar vs. mobile sheet), and allows the platform to evolve its design system without breaking plugins. A plugin never outputs HTML — it outputs JSON that the platform’s rendering engine transforms into UI components. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.5.1 Card Template
nodes.summary:
The document section describes the **Card** as the primary output format used to display structured information within a Side Panel interface. A Card includes a title, optional subtitle, icon, status indicator (info, success, warning, urgent), multiple content sections, action buttons, and an optional footer. Cards can be pinned, dismissed, or expanded by the user.

Each Card contains one or more **sections**, and each section supports different rendering styles:
- **text**: plain paragraph content  
- **key_value**: two-column label–value pairs  
- **list**: bullet-point format  
- **highlight**: emphasized callout box for important information  

The document also explains that action buttons (e.g., copy to clipboard, dismiss) can have different visual styles (primary, tertiary), and that visual presentation details such as colors and spacing are controlled by the platform’s design system, while the plugin defines only the content structure.

nodes.title: 12.5.2 Table Template
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Table Template**, a structured format used to render comparison grids and tabular data. It explains that the template is primarily used for scenarios such as product vs. competitor comparisons, tier comparisons for upselling, multi-product feature matrices for full solutions, and quote line items. Core agents supply the comparison data, and the plugin formats it into a standardized table layout.

The example demonstrates a tier comparison between Standard and Premium plans, showing configurable columns (with optional highlighting), feature-based rows, a summary statement highlighting key value differences, and optional user actions (such as copying content to clipboard). The template supports clear side-by-side comparisons, emphasis on recommended options, and actionable follow-ups.

nodes.title: 12.5.3 Form Template
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Form Template**, which is designed for plugins that require user input rather than just displaying output. The template allows a plugin to pre-populate form fields (using LLM-generated content or assembled data), enabling a representative to review and edit the information before submission.

When the user submits the form or selects an action, the updated form data is either sent back to the plugin’s `execute()` function (including the form state as context) or handled through built-in actions such as `copy_to_clipboard` or `re_execute`.

Common use cases include:
- Editing generated email drafts before sending or copying  
- Adjusting quote details (e.g., quantities, discounts) before generating a PDF  
- Custom data entry forms, such as warranty lookups using serial numbers  

The document provides a sample JSON structure for a form, including a title, multiple fields, and action buttons. Supported field types include: `text`, `textarea`, `email`, `number`, `dropdown`, `checkbox`, `date`, and `hidden`.

Each field can define:
- `id` (unique identifier)  
- `type`  
- `label`  
- `value` (default/pre-populated content)  
- `required` (boolean)  
- `options` (for dropdown fields)  
- `placeholder`  
- `validation` (such as regex patterns or min/max constraints)  

The template also supports configurable actions with labels, action types, and styles, enabling flexible interaction workflows.

nodes.title: 12.5.4 File Output
nodes.summary:
### 12.5.4 File Output

Some plugins produce downloadable files rather than (or in addition to) inline UI. Generate Quote produces a formatted quote document. Meeting Prep Brief might produce a printable one-page brief. The file output type returns a file reference that the UI renders as a download button.

| { "type": "file", "filename": "Quote_AcmeManufacturing_2026-03-04.pdf", "mimeType": "application/pdf", "data": "<base64-encoded-content>", "preview": {  // Optional inline preview card "type": "card", "title": "Quote: Acme Manufacturing", "sections": [{ "heading": "Summary", "content": "3 line items, total $24,500", "style": "text" }], "actions": [{ "label": "Download PDF", "action": "download_file" }] } } |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.5.5 Custom Component (Full Product Only)
nodes.summary:
This section defines the strategy for handling Custom Components in the platform’s UI system.

It explains that when standard templates (Card, Table, Form, and File) are insufficient, plugins in the full product (not MVP) may provide a custom React component. These components are rendered inside a tightly sandboxed iframe in the Side Panel with strict security constraints: only scripts are allowed, no same-origin access, no top-level navigation, no external resource loading due to a strict Content Security Policy, and communication with the platform exclusively via a structured postMessage API (no direct DOM access).

Custom Components are explicitly excluded from the MVP and reserved for complex, highly interactive use cases such as network diagrams, drag-and-drop builders, or scheduling widgets. Plugins using Custom Components undergo enhanced review, including security scanning of the React bundle, a 500KB size limit, and manual inspection for unsafe DOM manipulation.

The final decision establishes that the MVP will rely solely on the four predefined UI templates, which cover all built-in plugins. Custom Components are a full-product escape hatch for advanced scenarios, justified by the need for consistent UX, stronger security, adaptive rendering, and simpler plugin development through JSON-based outputs instead of custom UI code.

nodes.title: 12.6 Plugin Output Bus — Inter-Plugin Communication
nodes.summary:
This section explains the **Plugin Output Bus**, a mechanism that enables inter-plugin communication without creating direct dependencies between plugins.

Key points covered:

- **Purpose:** Plugins operate independently but can benefit from accessing each other’s results (e.g., Email Gen using data from a Competitor Card plugin). The Output Bus allows this safely and loosely coupled.

- **How it works:**  
  The Orchestrator maintains a `session.pluginOutputs` object for the session. When a plugin runs, its sanitized, rendered output is stored there. Other plugins can access this data using `context.pluginOutputs.read(pluginId)`.

- **Access model:**  
  - Plugins have **read-only access** to another plugin’s final rendered output (the same JSON sent to the UI).  
  - No access is granted to another plugin’s private `plugin_state`.

- **Restrictions:**  
  Plugins cannot:
  - Read another plugin’s private working state.
  - Modify another plugin’s output.
  - Invoke another plugin directly.
  - Create hard dependencies. If expected output is unavailable, the reading plugin must proceed gracefully (receives `null`).

- **Example use case:**  
  Email Gen reads a competitor comparison table from the Competitor Card plugin. If the data exists, it includes it in the email; if not, it continues without it.

Overall, the section emphasizes safe, read-only, loosely coupled data sharing between plugins to enhance functionality while preserving isolation and independence.

nodes.title: 12.7 Rep Interface Layout — Where Plugins Render
nodes.summary:
This section defines the Rep Interface Layout and explains where plugins render within the sales workflow UI. It clarifies the major interface zones and how each interacts with core system components versus plugins.

The **Customer Context Panel** (left panel) displays persistent customer information such as profile details, owned products, key contacts, and discovery progress. It is a core UI component that reads directly from system state and is not plugin-driven.

The **Accepted Products Tray** acts as a “shopping cart” for products the rep selects during the conversation. It is also a core UI element, not a plugin, and feeds data into downstream processes like quote generation.

The **Chat Panel** (center workspace) contains the main conversation between the rep and AI agents, including recommendations and discovery guidance. Plugins do not render directly in this area; it is reserved for the core agent workflow.

The **Side Panel** (right panel) is the primary plugin rendering zone. Plugin outputs—such as cards, tables, forms, files, or custom components—appear here as stackable, pinnable, or collapsible elements. Both auto-triggered and manually triggered plugins render in this space, ordered by priority.

The **Quick Action Bar** contains plugin trigger buttons. Some are always visible, while others appear contextually based on trigger conditions. Clicking a button executes the corresponding plugin.

Finally, the document notes that while the MVP relies on AI recommendations and a KB Search plugin for product selection, the full product will include a **Product Catalog Browser**. This allows reps to independently search, filter, and add products to the Accepted Products Tray without relying on AI-driven discovery, supporting more experienced sales workflows.

nodes.title: 12.8 Built-In Quick Actions — All 8 Plugins
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.8 Built-In Quick Actions — All 8 Plugins

All 8 built-in plugins are built on the same SDK described above. They are NOT special — they use the same manifest, execute function, Plugin Gateway, and rendering templates as any custom plugin. This section specifies each plugin’s trigger, data diet, output, LLM usage, and evolution during a conversation.

nodes.title: 12.8.1 Availability and Trigger Matrix
nodes.summary:
This section defines the **availability rules, trigger conditions, phase visibility, LLM usage, and priority order** for each plugin in the system.

It presents a **Trigger Matrix** outlining:

- **When each plugin’s button is visible** (e.g., always, session start, after specific signals).
- **Automatic trigger conditions** based on system signals such as:
  - Customer recognition
  - Competitor mentions
  - Use case or industry detection
  - Objection detection
  - Presence of recommendations or accepted products
- **Which sales phase(s)** each plugin appears in (Discovery, Recommendation, Action, or all phases).
- **Whether the plugin uses an LLM**.
- **Surface priority**, where lower numbers indicate higher priority in display order.

Key behaviors include:
- Some plugins are **manual only** (e.g., KB Search).
- Some trigger automatically at **session start** under specific conditions (e.g., Account Overview, Meeting Prep Brief).
- Others activate dynamically based on **intent signals or agent state changes** (e.g., Competitor Comparison, Objection Handler, Generate Quote).
  
The section also clarifies **simultaneous triggering behavior**:
- When multiple plugins trigger at the same time, **all are shown in the Side Panel**.
- They are ordered by **surfacePriority (ascending)**.
- The Orchestrator does **not** select a single plugin.
- The sales representative chooses which plugin to use, avoiding automated prioritization decisions by the platform.

nodes.title: 12.8.2 Per-Plugin Specification
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines detailed specifications for individual plugins within a sales assistant system, describing their purpose, data inputs, triggering logic, processing approach (LLM vs. retrieval vs. template-based), and output format.

Key points covered:

1. Clear Separation of Plugin Types  
   - Retrieval-only plugins (e.g., KB Search, Find Case Study) that use semantic search without LLM generation.  
   - Pure data assembly plugins (e.g., Account Overview, Generate Quote in MVP) that format pre-computed or catalog data without inference.  
   - LLM-powered synthesis plugins (e.g., Meeting Prep Brief, Competitor Comparison, Generate Email, Objection Handler) that combine structured data, KB queries, and conversation context to generate narrative or strategic outputs.

2. Defined Data Dependencies  
   Each plugin explicitly specifies what system data it reads, such as:
   - customer.profile, products, contacts  
   - enrichment metrics (health score, YoY growth, LTV, whitespace, benchmarks)  
   - agent_state (recommendations, talking points, session summaries)  
   - intent_signals (competitor mentions, objections)  
   - Conversation history (last N messages)  
   - KB queries via Foundry IQ  
   - Plugin Output Bus (cross-plugin data sharing)

3. Triggering Logic  
   Plugins are either:
   - Always available (manual trigger)  
   - Auto-surfaced at session start (e.g., Account Overview, Meeting Prep Brief under conditions)  
   - Triggered by NLU-detected signals (e.g., competitor mention, objection detection, discovery signals)  
   - Triggered after specific workflow steps (e.g., Generate Email after recommendations)

4. Structured Output Formats  
   Outputs are consistently defined as structured UI components:
   - Cards with list sections, key-value sections, highlight sections  
   - Tables (feature comparisons)  
   - Editable form templates (email, quote adjustments)  
   - File outputs (structured quote preview, future PDF support)

5. Sales Workflow Coverage  
   The plugins collectively support the full sales cycle:
   - Research & discovery (KB Search, Account Overview, Meeting Prep Brief)  
   - Competitive positioning (Competitor Comparison, Objection Handler)  
   - Social proof & validation (Find Case Study)  
   - Follow-up & communication (Generate Email)  
   - Commercial closing (Generate Quote)

6. Emphasis on Contextual Intelligence  
   Many plugins enhance outputs using:
   - Customer-specific data  
   - Industry matching  
   - Prior session summaries  
   - Conversation context  
   - Cross-plugin insights  

Overall, the document defines a modular, data-driven plugin architecture for a sales assistant, with strict rules on inputs, computation method, trigger conditions, and structured outputs to ensure consistency, explainability, and workflow alignment.

nodes.title: 12.8.3 Data Diet Summary
nodes.summary:
The section titled **“12.8.3 Data Diet Summary”** outlines how different system plugins utilize data, knowledge sources, conversation history, and LLM tokens. It presents a comparative table showing:

- **State Fields Used**: The specific customer data, agent state data, enrichment data, and intent signals each plugin accesses.
- **Knowledge Base Sources**: External sources such as case studies, competitor intelligence, and product catalogs that support each plugin.
- **History Depth**: The number of prior conversation messages each plugin considers.
- **LLM Token Usage**: The typical token consumption for each plugin, highlighting which functions require significant language model processing.

The table demonstrates that some plugins (e.g., Account Overview, Generate Quote, Find Case Study) operate without LLM token usage, relying purely on structured data, while others (e.g., Generate Email, Competitor Comparison, Meeting Prep Brief, Objection Handler) require substantial LLM processing. Overall, the section summarizes how data access and computational resources are allocated across different system capabilities.

nodes.title: 12.8.4 Deployment Strategy
nodes.summary:
### 12.8.4 Deployment Strategy

| DECISION: All Built-In Plugins Bundled in Orchestrator Service Decided: All 8 built-in plugins run within the Orchestrator service (Module 2), executed by the Plugin Gateway. They are NOT separate microservices. Each plugin is a function invocation, not a persistent process. Rationale: Plugins are short-lived (< 5 seconds), stateless functions. Deploying 8 separate services for 8 small functions is massive over-engineering — 8 Kubernetes pods, 8 pipelines, 8 health checks for functions that run 2–3 seconds each. The Plugin Gateway handles isolation via sandboxed execution contexts. Built-in code is trusted. Custom plugins in full product MAY run in isolated containers (Lambda/Azure Functions) because we don’t trust external code, but built-in plugins always execute in-process. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.9 Agent Manifest Control — Versioning, Customization, and Deployment
nodes.prefix_summary: ## 12.9 Agent Manifest Control — Versioning, Customization, and Deployment

nodes.title: 12.9.1 Where Manifests Live
nodes.summary:
The document section explains where plugin manifests are stored and how they are managed for both built-in and custom plugins.

For built-in plugins, manifest files are stored in the codebase under `/plugins/{plugin_id}/manifest.json`. During platform deployment, the CI/CD pipeline reads these manifest files and registers or updates them in the `plugin_registry` database table.

For custom plugins (in the full product version), manifests are submitted through the Admin Portal. These are stored in the `plugin_registry` table with an associated `tenant_id`, and their code bundles are stored separately in the tenant’s Blob Storage container.

The section also defines the schema of the `plugin_registry` table. It includes fields such as `plugin_id`, `tenant_id` (null for built-in plugins), `version`, `manifest` (stored as JSONB), `status` (with a lifecycle from pending_review to deprecated), `code_bundle_url`, timestamps, approval metadata, and a uniqueness constraint on `(plugin_id, tenant_id, version)`.

nodes.title: 12.9.2 Are Built-In Plugins Domain-Specific?
nodes.summary:
The document explains that built-in plugins are domain-agnostic by design, meaning they function the same way across all industries. The plugin logic does not change based on industry; instead, only the data they operate on is tenant-specific. For example, tools like Email Gen and Competitor Card use tenant-specific data (such as customer profiles, recommendations, and knowledge base content), but their underlying code remains universal.

Domain-specific behavior does not come from the plugins themselves. Instead, it is driven by three external factors: (1) tenant-specific prompt modifiers injected into LLM calls to adjust tone and terminology, (2) tenant business rules enforced by the Orchestrator before and after plugin execution, and (3) tenant-specific knowledge base content that produces different results for each tenant.

nodes.title: 12.9.3 Tenant Customization — Three Levels
nodes.summary:
The document explains a three-level model for tenant customization within a multi-tenant plugin-based system, emphasizing that there are no code branches per tenant.

**Level 1: Prompt Modifiers** allow tenants to customize LLM behavior (tone, terminology, domain instructions) through configuration. These are stored as per-tenant data and do not require code changes or deployment. All tenants share the same codebase, eliminating branch risk.

**Level 2: Template Overrides** enable tenants to modify the structure of plugin outputs (e.g., form fields, table columns, layout sections). These changes are also configuration-driven, stored per tenant, and applied at runtime. Again, no code branching or deployments are required.

**Level 3: Custom Plugin Forks** allow tenants to build and maintain entirely separate plugins using an SDK. These custom plugins are independently owned and stored by the tenant. While they involve code deployment, it is the tenant’s responsibility and does not affect the core product or create branching risk for the platform.

The key architectural principle is that the platform maintains a single version of each built-in plugin. Tenant differences are handled through configuration (Levels 1–2) or fully separate custom plugins (Level 3). This ensures seamless upgrades—when a built-in plugin is updated, all tenants receive the update with their configurations automatically applied, avoiding merge conflicts or version fragmentation.

Additionally, plugin availability can be controlled per tenant using a configuration list of enabled plugin IDs. Individual users can further personalize their experience by hiding specific plugins at the user level, separate from tenant-level enablement.

nodes.title: 12.10 Feedback and Analytics — What We Collect and How We Use It
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.10 Feedback and Analytics — What We Collect and How We Use It

| Connection to Module 16 Plugin analytics feed into Module 16 (Feedback Engine), which is the platform’s unified feedback processing system. This section defines WHAT signals plugins generate. Module 16 defines HOW those signals are aggregated, analyzed, and used for system-wide improvement. The signals defined here are the plugin-specific subset of Module 16’s full signal taxonomy. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.10.1 Signal Taxonomy
nodes.summary:
The document section outlines a structured framework for tracking, evaluating, and optimizing plugin performance within a system.

It defines a **Signal Taxonomy** that categorizes data collected from plugin usage into five major signal groups:

1. **Execution Metrics** – Automatically captured system-level data (e.g., execution count, latency, token usage, errors, trigger type) used for monitoring health, performance optimization, cost tracking, and error alerting.

2. **Engagement Signals** – UI-tracked behavioral metrics (e.g., whether output was used or dismissed, interaction timing, dwell time) that measure perceived usefulness and help refine trigger conditions and plugin relevance.

3. **Edit Signals (Form Outputs)** – Detailed modification tracking (e.g., fields edited, edit distance, characters added/removed, regeneration count, final action) used to assess output quality and identify where prompt or generation improvements are needed.

4. **Dismiss Reasons (Optional Qualitative Feedback)** – User-provided explanations for dismissing outputs (e.g., not relevant, wrong timing) that support tuning of trigger logic, context matching, and personalization.

5. **Outcome Correlation (Full Product Scope)** – Cross-referencing plugin usage with downstream outcomes (e.g., recommendation acceptance, session duration, deal win/loss data) to measure ROI and business impact.

Additionally, the section describes **LLM Cost Tracking and Token Budget Management**, where token consumption is tracked per plugin and tenant. Administrators can set monthly budgets, and if exceeded, the system degrades gracefully to template-based outputs while notifying users. This ensures cost control and sustainable LLM usage.

nodes.title: 12.10.2 How Feedback Improves Plugins
nodes.summary:
This section explains how feedback improves plugin performance across different timeframes and levels of system maturity.

In real-time (within the same session), plugins automatically adapt using an `onFeedback` handler. For example, if a user clicks “Regenerate” in an email generator, the plugin adjusts the next output based on session memory, such as changing tone. This is handled automatically by the plugin itself.

In the weekly MVP stage, engineers manually review aggregated usage metrics (such as edit rates) from dashboards. If patterns emerge—like high subject line edits for a specific industry—they update prompt modifiers in the tenant configuration to improve results.

In the full product version, automated systems (e.g., Module 16) analyze patterns and propose improvements. For instance, if a feature is frequently dismissed, the system may suggest disabling it or improving underlying knowledge quality. These proposals are reviewed and approved by tenant admins or engineers.

Additionally, A/B testing is used in the full product stage to compare prompt versions over time. Metrics such as edit rate and regeneration frequency determine the winning version, which is then set as default. Engineers configure the tests, Module 16 tracks performance, and engineers finalize the implementation.

Overall, the section outlines a progression from automatic session-level adjustments to data-driven manual improvements and eventually to automated optimization and experimentation.

nodes.title: 12.11.1 Step 1: Develop
nodes.summary:
This section describes Step 1: Develop in the plugin creation process.

It explains that the developer (either the internal team for built-in plugins or tenant developers for custom ones) must implement three key files:

- **manifest.json**: Defines the plugin’s configuration and acts as a contract. It specifies triggers, permissions, resources, output schema, and feedback signals. The Plugin Gateway uses it to provision the execution environment, enforce permissions, and validate outputs.
- **execute.ts**: Contains the main business logic. It receives a `PluginContext` and returns structured output that matches the defined `outputSchema`. This file handles data assembly, LLM calls, formatting, and conditional logic.
- **onFeedback.ts (optional)**: Handles real-time feedback for session-based adjustments. It is typically used in plugins that require regeneration or iterative refinement (e.g., Email Generator or Objection Handler).

The section also notes that developers use the `@sip/plugin-sdk` TypeScript package for type checking, which provides types for contexts, output schemas, feedback signals, and API clients. However, the SDK is compile-time only; the runtime implementation is injected by the Plugin Gateway.

nodes.title: 12.11.2 Step 2: Test
nodes.summary:
The document section describes **Step 2: Testing** of a plugin using the **Plugin Test Harness**, a local CLI tool included in `@sip/plugin-sdk` that simulates the Plugin Gateway.

It explains how developers:

- **Load mock context data** (e.g., fake customer data, recommendations, KB results) into a JSON file that acts as the `PluginContext`.
- **Execute the plugin against the mock context** using the `execute(mockContext)` function and capture results.
- **Validate the output schema**, ensuring required fields, correct data types, proper section styles, and size limits.
- **Enforce permission compliance** by wrapping context data in a permission proxy that throws errors if undeclared state fields are accessed.
- **Measure performance**, checking execution time against `maxExecutionMs`, and optionally using either mock or real LLM calls for testing.
- **Test edge cases**, such as missing data, empty knowledge bases, LLM timeouts, or unavailable contacts, ensuring graceful fallback behavior instead of errors.

An example CLI test run is shown, demonstrating validation checks (schema, permissions, execution time, API limits), edge case handling, and a final confirmation that all tests passed and the plugin is ready for registration.

nodes.title: 12.11.3 Step 3: Register
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.3 Step 3: Register

Built-in plugins: Registration is automatic. The CI/CD pipeline reads /plugins/*/manifest.json and upserts into plugin_registry. Status is set to ‘active’ immediately (no review gate for built-in).

Custom plugins (full product): Tenant admin uploads the plugin bundle (manifest + code) via Admin Portal. The bundle is validated (schema compliance, size limits, required fields). The manifest is parsed and inserted into plugin_registry with status: ‘pending_review.’

nodes.title: 12.11.4 Step 4: Review (Full Product Custom Plugins Only)
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.4 Step 4: Review (Full Product Custom Plugins Only)

Built-in plugins skip this step entirely. Custom plugins undergo review before activation:

Manifest audit: Does it declare only the permissions it actually needs? Is externalNetwork: true justified? Are resource limits reasonable?

Code review: Does the code do what the manifest says? Any hidden API calls? Any data exfiltration attempts? Any attempt to access DOM or browser APIs?

Security scan: Automated static analysis for common vulnerabilities: injection patterns, eval() usage, external URL construction, obfuscated code.

Test results: Did it pass the test harness? All edge cases handled? Performance within limits?

Review result: approved (status changes to ‘approved’, can be activated by tenant admin) or rejected with specific feedback for the developer to address.

nodes.title: 12.11.5 Step 5: Deploy / Activate
nodes.summary:
### 12.11.5 Step 5: Deploy / Activate

Built-in plugins: Deployed with every platform release. Available to all tenants. Whether a specific plugin is ENABLED for a tenant depends on tenant_config.agent_config.quick_action_ids.

Custom plugins: After approval, tenant admin activates the plugin in Admin Portal. Status changes from ‘approved’ to ‘active.’ The Orchestrator’s plugin trigger evaluation now includes this plugin for this tenant’s sessions.

Rollback: If a plugin update introduces a regression, the previous version can be re-activated. plugin_registry stores version history. Rollback = deactivate current version, activate previous version. One database update, immediate effect for new sessions.

nodes.title: 12.11.6 Step 6: Monitor
nodes.summary:
This section explains how plugin performance is monitored after deployment. Each plugin execution is logged and tracked through a monitoring dashboard that provides visibility into per-plugin health and usage patterns.

Key metrics include:

- **Usage frequency**: How often each plugin is triggered (automatically or manually) and whether users interact with or dismiss it.
- **Dismissal rate**: The percentage of auto-triggered plugins dismissed without interaction; rates above 60% are flagged for review.
- **Edit rate (for form plugins)**: The percentage of generated outputs that users modify before use; high edit rates on specific fields indicate potential quality issues.
- **Error rate**: The percentage of failed executions (e.g., timeouts, LLM errors, schema validation failures); rates above 5% trigger engineering alerts.
- **LLM cost**: Token usage per plugin and per tenant, tracked monthly to support cost analysis and reporting.

A circuit breaker mechanism is also described: if a plugin fails three consecutive times within a session, it is automatically disabled for the remainder of that session and an alert is logged. Other plugins continue functioning normally, and the disabled plugin is re-enabled in the next session.

nodes.title: 12.12 Alternative Architecture: Open Plugin Framework
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 12.12 Alternative Architecture: Open Plugin Framework

| Why This Section Exists The Controlled Framework (Sections 12.1–12.11) prioritizes safety, consistency, and predictability. It is the recommended approach for MVP and early full product. However, as the platform matures and the developer ecosystem grows, a more open framework may be warranted. This section presents an alternative architecture that trades some control for developer freedom. The constraint is: security isolation and analytics collection remain mandatory. Everything else is negotiable. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 12.12.1 Philosophy Shift
nodes.summary:
### Section 12.12.1 – Philosophy Shift

This section outlines a fundamental shift from a tightly controlled, platform-governed plugin framework to a more open, flexible, and developer-empowered architecture. It compares the earlier “Controlled Framework” (Sections 12.1–12.11) with the new “Open Framework” introduced here, highlighting expanded capabilities and relaxed constraints across several dimensions.

**1. UI Output Flexibility**  
Previously, plugins were restricted to predefined UI templates (Card, Table, Form, File), with custom components heavily sandboxed. In the open model, plugins can render full React components directly. While a platform component library is provided, developers are free to create custom UI elements. Security is maintained through iframe sandboxing and a postMessage API.

**2. LLM Access Model**  
Under the controlled framework, all LLM calls were mediated by the platform via built-in or declared connectors. In the open framework, plugins can directly integrate any LLM SDK (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic) without platform mediation. The platform still offers a built-in connector for convenience and tracks token usage through lightweight instrumentation.

**3. State Access Permissions**  
The earlier model required explicit declaration of every field-level read permission, with strict write isolation. The open framework relaxes read restrictions—plugins can access any non-sensitive state without prior declaration. Write access expands to a shared plugin namespace (`plugin_shared.*`), while core system state remains protected.

**4. Plugin-to-Plugin Interaction**  
Previously, plugins could only read other plugins’ rendered output in a read-only manner, with no direct invocation. The open framework enables direct inter-plugin communication via a message bus. Plugins can invoke each other’s `execute()` functions, enabling orchestrated workflows. Circular dependencies are detected and prevented.

**5. Review and Approval Process**  
The controlled framework required manual code review for all custom plugins. The open framework shifts to automated security scanning and manifest auditing. Manual review is reserved for higher-risk plugins—those requesting external network access, shared state writes, or custom components—while low-risk plugins can be auto-approved.

**6. Resource Limits**  
Hard, strictly enforced limits (timeouts, read counts, query size, LLM calls) characterized the controlled framework. The open framework introduces soft limits with burst allowances. Plugins can request extended execution time (up to 30 seconds with justification), perform more reads and queries, and make multiple LLM calls.

Overall, this section describes a move from a highly restricted, centrally governed plugin system to a more open, extensible, and developer-friendly ecosystem—while retaining targeted safeguards around security, core state protection, and risk-based review.

nodes.title: 12.12.2 Open Framework Security Model
nodes.summary: The section outlines the non-negotiable security constraints within the Open Framework Security Model. It emphasizes three absolute protections: strict tenant data isolation enforced at database, API, and execution levels; mandatory analytics collection for every plugin execution, preventing any tampering or bypass to ensure full system optimization visibility; and enforced output sanitization through iframe sandboxing, which blocks direct DOM access, external resource loading, and access to cookies or local storage. These measures ensure strong security, data separation, monitoring integrity, and containment of plugin behavior regardless of the framework’s openness.

nodes.title: 12.12.3 Open Framework LLM Access
nodes.summary:
This section describes how the open framework allows plugins to use their own large language models (LLMs) instead of being limited to the platform’s built-in option. While the platform provides a default connector (`context.llm.call()`), plugins can import and use any external LLM SDK (such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cohere), manage their own encrypted API keys, and select specialized or fine-tuned models tailored to specific tenant needs (e.g., healthcare or compliance-focused models).

All LLM interactions—whether through the built-in connector or external providers—are automatically wrapped by a mandatory instrumentation layer. This wrapper logs metadata such as the model used, token consumption, latency, and estimated cost. The instrumentation is injected by the Plugin Gateway at runtime and cannot be bypassed.

The section also highlights security controls for external LLM usage. Plugins must declare external LLM endpoints in their manifest, and the Plugin Gateway enforces endpoint whitelisting. All outbound requests are logged, and tenant administrators can monitor external LLM usage through analytics dashboards. Additionally, tenants with strict data residency or compliance requirements can disable external LLM access entirely through configuration settings.

nodes.title: 12.12.4 Open Framework State Access
nodes.summary:
This section describes the **Open Framework State Access** model for plugins.

Key points:

- **Broader Read Access:** Plugins can read entire namespaces (`customer.*`, `enrichment.*`, `intent_signals.*`) without declaring individual fields. Access is granted at the namespace level via the manifest. However, sensitive data such as authentication tokens, tenant configuration internals, and system prompts remain restricted by the Plugin Gateway.

- **Shared Plugin State:** Beyond their own private state (`plugin_state.{own_id}.*`), plugins can write to a shared namespace (`plugin_shared.*`) accessible to all plugins. This enables cross-plugin collaboration (e.g., one plugin writes selected products and others read them). If multiple plugins write to the same field, conflicts are resolved using a last-write-wins strategy based on timestamps.

- **Protected Core State:** Certain critical namespaces (`agent_state.*`, `discovery.*`, `active_workflow`, and `recommendations.*`) are strictly read-only for plugins. Only the Orchestrator and core agents are allowed to modify these core platform states, even under the open framework.

nodes.title: 12.12.5 Migration Path: Controlled to Open
nodes.summary:
This section outlines a phased migration strategy from a Controlled Framework to an Open Framework.

**Phase 1 (MVP)** starts with a fully controlled environment: only built-in plugins, predefined templates (Card/Table/Form/File), a built-in LLM, read-only state, and no custom plugins. The goal is to validate the SDK, build confidence, and establish operational baselines.

**Phase 2 (Full Product v1)** introduces controlled extensibility. Tenant developers can create custom plugins using the same SDK, subject to manual review. A sandboxed State Write API and iframe-based custom components are added. This phase enables tenant innovation while maintaining strong guardrails.

**Phase 3 (Full Product v2)** transitions to an Open Framework. It expands permissions to include broader state access, external LLM connectors, direct plugin invocation via a message bus, automated security scanning, and a shared plugin namespace. This phase is triggered only after sufficient production maturity (10+ custom plugins, no security incidents, and demonstrated tenant demand).

The key decision is to begin with the Controlled Framework for MVP and early releases, prioritizing safety, simplicity, and proven demand. The architecture is intentionally designed so that moving to the Open Framework is a permissions expansion—not a system rewrite—since core components like the Plugin Gateway, manifest system, and analytics remain consistent across phases.

nodes.title: 12.13 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary:
The document summarizes key architectural and product decisions behind the Plugin SDK and plugin ecosystem design.

First, the SDK is defined as an interface contract rather than a standalone library or independent service. Plugins are TypeScript-defined functions executed inside a centralized Plugin Gateway within the Orchestrator. This ensures consistent execution, simplified deployment, and strict permission control managed by the Gateway.

Second, built-in plugins and custom plugins use the exact same SDK with no privileged APIs or backdoors. This “dogfooding” approach ensures the SDK is production-ready, builds trust with tenant developers, and guarantees that any new capability added for internal use becomes available to all.

Third, plugins are designed to be domain-agnostic. Industry-specific behavior is injected at runtime through tenant configuration (prompts, knowledge base content, business rules). This avoids maintaining multiple industry-specific plugin variants and ensures improvements benefit all tenants immediately.

Fourth, the MVP uses template-based UI components (Card, Table, Form, File) to cover most use cases with consistent UX and strong security. Custom React components (iframe-sandboxed) are reserved for the full product as a controlled escape hatch once the security infrastructure is mature.

Fifth, all plugin feedback is routed into a single unified Feedback Engine rather than separate per-plugin systems. This enables cross-component pattern detection and systemic improvements that would be missed with isolated feedback loops.

Finally, the framework follows a controlled-first approach. The initial product restricts permissions through a tightly governed SDK, with plans to open the framework later once demand and security stability are proven. The architecture is designed so expansion is additive rather than requiring a redesign.
